items.followUp: State two differences between Rutherford’s and Bohr’s atomic models.

rubric.why: Assesses Rutherford’s description of the nucleus and electrons.
rubric.description: Rutherford proposed a positively charged nucleus with electrons revolving around it.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the positively charged nucleus and revolving electrons.

rubric.why: Assesses a limitation of Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: Rutherford’s model did not describe fixed electron energy levels and could not explain atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award for either stating that fixed energy levels were not described or that the model could not explain atomic stability.

rubric.why: Assesses Bohr’s proposed arrangement of electrons.
rubric.description: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy specific fixed orbits, each with a definite energy.
rubric.how: Award for stating that Bohr proposed fixed orbits or energy levels for electrons.

rubric.why: Assesses Bohr’s explanation of atomic stability and energy transitions.
rubric.description: Electrons do not radiate energy in stationary orbits; they absorb or emit energy when moving between energy levels.
rubric.how: Award for the no-radiation rule for stationary orbits or for energy absorption/emission during transitions.

modelAnswer: Rutherford proposed that an atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus, with electrons revolving around it.
Rutherford’s model did not describe fixed energy levels for the electrons and could not explain the stability of the atom.
Bohr proposed that electrons revolve around the nucleus in specific fixed orbits, each having a definite energy.
Electrons do not radiate energy while in these stationary orbits; they absorb or emit energy when they move between energy levels.

items.followUp: Differentiate between polar and non-polar covalent bonds, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Assesses the unequal sharing that makes a covalent bond polar.
rubric.description: In a polar covalent bond, the bonded atoms share the electron pair unequally.
rubric.how: Award for identifying unequal sharing in a polar covalent bond.

rubric.why: Assesses the charge separation and example for a polar bond.
rubric.description: Unequal sharing creates partial positive and negative charges; HCl is an example.
rubric.how: Award for describing the partial charges and giving a valid polar-bond example.

rubric.why: Assesses the equal sharing that makes a covalent bond non-polar.
rubric.description: In a non-polar covalent bond, the bonded atoms share the electron pair equally, so no poles develop.
rubric.how: Award for identifying equal sharing and the absence of poles.

rubric.why: Assesses an appropriate example of a non-polar covalent bond.
rubric.description: Cl₂, H₂ or O₂ is an example of a non-polar covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award for giving a valid non-polar covalent-bond example.

modelAnswer: In a polar covalent bond, the bonded atoms share the electron pair unequally, so partial positive charges and partial negative charges develop; HCl is an example.
In a non-polar covalent bond, the bonded atoms share the electron pair equally, so no poles develop; Cl₂ is an example.

items.followUp: Define vapour pressure and explain how temperature and intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Assesses the essential conditions in the definition of vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by vapours in equilibrium with their liquid at a particular temperature.
rubric.how: Award for stating that vapour exerts pressure while in equilibrium with its liquid.

rubric.why: Assesses the effect of temperature on vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Increasing temperature increases vapour pressure because more liquid particles escape into the vapour phase.
rubric.how: Award for stating that vapour pressure increases as temperature increases.

rubric.why: Assesses the effect of weaker intermolecular attractions.
rubric.description: Liquids with weaker intermolecular forces evaporate more readily and have higher vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award for relating weaker intermolecular forces to higher vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Assesses the contrasting effect of stronger intermolecular attractions.
rubric.description: Stronger intermolecular forces give lower vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award for relating stronger intermolecular forces to lower vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Assesses the effect of a non-volatile solute on vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Dissolving a non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of a liquid.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a non-volatile solute decreases vapour pressure.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapours of a liquid when they are in equilibrium with the liquid at a particular temperature.
Temperature: On increasing temperature, more liquid particles gain enough energy to escape into the vapour phase, so vapour pressure increases.
Nature of the liquid: Liquids with weaker intermolecular forces evaporate more readily and have higher vapour pressure; stronger forces give lower vapour pressure.
Nonvolatile solute: Dissolving a nonvolatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of the liquid.

items.followUp: Define organic chemistry and inorganic chemistry.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition of physical chemistry.
rubric.description: Physical chemistry deals with the physical properties and behaviour of matter and the energy changes involved in chemical processes.
rubric.how: Award for defining physical chemistry in terms of matter’s physical properties or behaviour, or energy changes in chemical processes.

rubric.why: Assesses the definition of nuclear chemistry.
rubric.description: Nuclear chemistry deals with changes in atomic nuclei and the associated nuclear reactions.
rubric.how: Award for identifying atomic nuclei or nuclear reactions as the subject of nuclear chemistry.

modelAnswer: Physical chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the physical properties and behaviour of matter and the energy changes involved in chemical processes.
Nuclear chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with changes in the nuclei of atoms and the nuclear reactions associated with them.
